h: Beaches, brochs and a night in a blackhouse
p: The people of Gearrannan lived in these blackhouses until the 1970s, when the last residents moved out to more modern homes. The village was then lovingly restored, and it now gives visitors a real sense of how a whole community lived together on this exposed stretch of the Atlantic coast. Wander between the houses and look at how they sit low into the land, tucked against the weather with thick double walls packed with earth.

If you've got time, consider staying overnight. Some of the restored houses are let as self-catering cottages and a hostel, and falling asleep with the sound of the sea outside is a memory that sticks. It's also the best way to see the village at its most peaceful, after the day's visitors have gone.

The west coast of Lewis is packed with sights within a short drive. Dun Carloway is an incredibly well-preserved Iron Age broch, and at Shawbost you'll find a restored Norse-style mill and kiln in a quiet glen. Dalmore and Dalbeg are sheltered sandy beaches nearby, beautiful on a fine day, though the sea can be powerful so take care. Combine a few of these with the Callanish Stones and you've got a full day of Hebridean history.

Stornoway is the island's main town, about half an hour away, with shops, places to eat and the ferry to Ullapool. Look out for Harris Tweed while you're here, still woven by hand in homes across the islands, and you'll understand why it's become a symbol of island life.
